## Expected Value (Expectation)

::: {.callout title="Definition 11.1"}
The **expected value** or population mean of a random variable is one measure of centrality for a variable. It represents the center of mass of the distribution.

For a random variable $X$, it is denoted by $\text{E}[X]$ or $\mu_X$.

For discrete $X$ this is

$$
\mu_X = \text{E}[X] = \sum_{x\in \mathcal{X}} x \cdot P_X(x)
$$

For continuous $X$ this is

$$
\mu_X = \text{E}[X] = \int_{x\in \mathcal{X}} x \cdot f_X(x) \ dx
$$
:::

## Ex: Weighted Die

::: {.callout title="Example 11.1"}
Consider a four-sided weighted die with weights 0.25, 0.15, 0.35, and 0.25. This is represented by the random variable $X$ with PMF:

$$
P_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
0.25 &\text{ for } x = 1 \\
0.15 &\text{ for } x = 2 \\
0.35 &\text{ for } x = 3 \\
0.25 &\text{ for } x = 4 \\
0 &\text{ otherwise }
\end{cases}
$$

What is $\text{E}[X]$?
:::

. . .

$$
\text{E}[X] = 0.25 \times 1 + 0.15 \times 2 + 0.35 \times 3 + 0.25 \times 4 = 2.6
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
values <- 1:4
weights <- c(0.25, 0.15, 0.35, 0.25)

sum(values*weights)
```

## Ex: Discrete Expectation

::: {.callout title="Example 11.2"}
Let the discrete random variable $X$ have the following PMF:

$$
P_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
\frac{3-x}{6} &\text{for } x = 0, 1, 2, 3 \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

What is $\text{E}[X]$?
:::

. . .

By definition, $\text{E}[X]$ is

$$
\text{E}[X] = \sum_{x=0}^3 x \cdot \frac{3-x}{6} = 0 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + 1 \cdot \frac{1}{3} + 2 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 3 \cdot \frac{0}{6} =
\frac{2}{3}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
PX <- function(x){
  (3-x)/6
}

x <- 0:3
sum(x*PX(x))
```

## Ex: Cont. Expection (2)

::: {.callout title="Example 11.4"}
Let $X$ be a random variable with PDF:

$$
f_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
e^{-x} &\text{for } x \in (0, \infty) \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

What is $\text{E}[X]$?
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[X] &= \int_0^\infty x e^{-x} dx \\
&= \left[-x e^{-x}\right]_0^\infty + \int_0^\infty e^{-x} dx &\text{Integration by Parts}\\
&= \lim_{x\rightarrow \infty} -xe^{-x} + \left[-e^{-x}\right]_0^\infty \\
&= \lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} e^{-x} - \lim_{x \rightarrow \infty} e^{-x} + e^{-0} = 1 &\text{ L'Hopitals Rule}
\end{align}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
integrate(function(x) x*exp(-x), lower = 0, upper = Inf)
```

## Expectation of Functions of Random Variables

::: {.callout title="Definition 11.2"}
Let $X$ be a random variable and let $g(X)$ be some function of $X$. The **expected value** of $g(X)$, $\text{E}[g(X)]$ is computed as

$$
\mu_{g(X)} = \text{E}[g(X)] = \sum_{x\in \mathcal{X}} g(x) \cdot P_X(x) \text{ for discrete } X
$$

and

$$
\mu_{g(X)} = \text{E}[g(X)] = \int_{x\in \mathcal{X}} g(x) \cdot f_X(x) \ dx \text{ for continuous } X
$$
:::

## Variance

::: {.callout title="Definition 11.3"}
The **variance** of a random variable $X$, $\text{Var}[X]$ is defined as

$$
\sigma^2_X = \text{Var}[X] = \text{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} (x-\mu)^2 \cdot P_X(x) \text{ for discrete X}
$$

and

$$
\sigma^2_X = \text{Var}[X] = \text{E}[(X-\mu)^2] = \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} (x-\mu)^2 \cdot f_X(x) \ dx \text{ for continuous X}
$$
:::

This expression simplifies to $\text{E}[g(X)]$ when $g(X) = (X-\mu)^2$.

## Ex: Discrete Variance

::: {.callout title="Example 11.5"}
Let the discrete random variable $X$ have the following PMF:

$$
P_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
\frac{3-x}{6} &\text{for } x = 0, 1, 2, 3 \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

What is $\text{Var}[X]$?
:::

. . .

By definition, we have that $\text{Var}[X]$ is

$$
\text{Var}[X] = \sum_{x=0}^3 \left(x-\frac{2}{3}\right)^2 \cdot \frac{3-x}{6} = \frac{4}{9} \cdot \frac{1}{2} + \frac{1}{9} \cdot \frac{1}{3} + \frac{16}{9} \cdot \frac{1}{6} + \frac{49}{9} \cdot \frac{0}{6} =
\frac{5}{9}
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
PX <- function(x){
  (3-x)/6
}

x <- 0:3
sum((x-2/3)^2*PX(x))
```

## Expectations of Linear Transformations

::: {.callout title="Theorem 11.1"}
The expected value of any function of a random variable $X$ of the form $g(X) = aX + b$ is:

$$
\text{E}[aX+b] = a\text{E}[X] + b
$$
:::

## Expectations of Linear Transformations (Proof)

The proof in the continuous case is:

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[aX + b] &= \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} (ax+b) \cdot f_X(x) \ dx \\
&= a\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} x \cdot f_X(x) \ dx + b\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} f_X(x) \ dx \\
&= a\text{E}[X] + b
\end{align}
$$

. . .

The proof in the discrete case is similar:

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[aX + b] &= \sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} (ax+b) \cdot P_X(x) \ dx \\
&= a\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} x \cdot P_X(x) \ dx + b\sum_{x \in \mathcal{X}} P_X(x) \ dx \\
&= a\text{E}[X] + b
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Linear Expectation

::: {.callout title="Example 11.7"}
Let the continuous random variable $X$ have the following PDF:

$$
f_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
3 x^2 &\text{for } x \in (0, 1) \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Let $g(X) = 3X + 2$. What is $\text{E}[g(X)] = \text{E}[3X + 2]$?
:::

. . .

$$
\text{E}[3X + 2] = \int_0^1 (3x + 2) \cdot 3x^2 \ dx = \left[\frac{9}{4} x^4 + 2 x^3 \right]_0^1 \simeq 4.25
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
fX <- function(x){
  3*x^2
}

integrate(function(x) (3*x + 2)*fX(x), lower = 0, upper = 1)
```

## Ex: Linear Expectation, Continued

::: {.callout title="Example 11.7 (Continued)"}
Let the continuous random variable $X$ have the following PDF:

$$
f_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
3 x^2 &\text{for } x \in (0, 1) \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Let $g(X) = 3X + 2$. What is $\text{E}[g(X)] = \text{E}[3X + 2]$?
:::

. . .

We know that $\text{E}[X] = \frac{3}{4}$. From the linearity of expectations, we get that this is:

$$
\text{E}[3X + 2] = 3\text{E}[X] + 2 = 3\frac{3}{4} + 2 = 4.25
$$

## Ex: Sales

::: {.callout title="Example 11.8"}
Let $X$ be a random variable representing the number of products sold in a day. Assume we know that $\text{E}[X] = 4$. Assume that each day you have a base pay of \$100, whether you sell products or not. Also assume that you can make another \$50 for each product that you sell. How much can you expect to make on any given day?
:::

. . .

The amount made in a day is $g(X) = 50X + 100$. Then we have:

$$
\text{E}[g(X)] = 50\times\text{E}[X] + 100 = 50\times4 + 100 = 300
$$

## Ex: Procedure

Let $X$ be a random variable representing the time it takes to complete an elective medical procedure (in hours, minutes, etc.). Assume that the baseline cost for the procedure is \$2,000 and every hour the procedure lasts cost \$200. If the expected duration of the procedure is 4 hours, what is the expected cost for the elective procedure?

## Variance of Linear Transformations

::: {.callout title="Theorem 11.2"}
The variance of any function of a random variable $X$ of the form $g(X) = aX + b$ is:

$$
\text{Var}[aX+b] = a^2\text{Var}[X]
$$
:::

## Variance of Linear Transformations (Proof)

The proof for the continuous case is as follows:

$$
\begin{align}
\text{Var}[aX + b] &= \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \left((ax+b)-\text{E}[(ax-b)]\right)^2 \cdot f_X(x) \ dx \\
&= \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \left(ax-a\mu\right)^2 \cdot f_X(x) \ dx \\
&= a^2\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \left(x-\mu\right)^2 \cdot f_X(x) \ dx \\
&= a^2 \text{Var}[X]
\end{align}
$$

. . .

The proof for the discrete case is similar.

## Ex: Linear Variance

::: {.callout title="Example 11.10"}
Let the continuous random variable $X$ have the following PDF:

$$
f_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
3 x^2 &\text{for } x \in (0, 1) \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

What is $\text{Var}[3X + 2]$?
:::

. . .

We already know that $\text{Var}[X] = \frac{3}{80}$. So then the variance of $3X + 2$ is

$$
\text{Var}[3X+2] = 3^2 \text{Var}[X] = 9 \cdot \frac{3}{80} = \frac{27}{80}
$$

## Ex: Sales

::: {.callout title="Example 11.11"}
Let $X$ be a random variable representing the number of products sold in a day. Assume we know that $\text{Var}[X] = 4$. Assume that each day you have a base pay of \$100, whether you sell products or not. Also assume that you can make another \$50 for each product that you sell. What is the variability in sales for each day?
:::

. . .

Again, the amount made is given by $g(X) = 50X + 100$. However, now we want to find $\text{Var}[g(X)]$ which is:

$$
\text{Var}[g(X)] = 50^2 \times \text{Var}[X] = 50^2 \times 4 = 10000
$$

## Ex: Procedure

Assume that the baseline cost for the procedure is \$2,000 and every hour the procedure lasts cost \$200. If the variability in the duration of the procedure is 2 hours, what is the variability in the cost for the elective procedure?

## Ex: Nonlinear Expectation (1)

::: {.callout title="Example 11.13"}
Let the discrete random variable $X$ have the following PMF:

$$
P_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
\frac{3-x}{6} &\text{for } x = 0, 1, 2, 3 \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

and let $g(X) = X^2$. What is $\text{E}[g(X)] = \text{E}[X^2]$?
:::

. . .

By definition, we have that $\text{E}[g(X)]$ is

$$
\text{E}[X^2] = \sum_{x=0}^3 x^2 \cdot \frac{3-x}{6} = 0 \cdot \frac{1}{2} + 1 \cdot \frac{1}{3} + 4 \cdot \frac{1}{6} + 9 \cdot \frac{0}{6} =
1
$$

```{r, echo = TRUE}
PX <- function(X){ (3-x)/6 }
x <- 0:3
sum(x^2*PX(x))
```

## Ex: Nonlinear Expectation (2)

::: {.callout title="Example 11.14"}
Let the continuous random variable $X$ have the following PDF:

$$
f_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
(a+1)(a+2) \ x^a (1-x) &\text{for } x \in (0, 1) \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Let $g(X) = X^2$. What is $\text{E}[g(X)] = \text{E}[X^2]$?
:::

. . .

$$
\begin{align}
\text{E}[X^2] &= \int_0^1 x^2 \cdot (a+1)(a+2) \ x^a (1-x) \ dx  \\
&= (a+1)(a+2) \int_0^1 x^{a+2} - x^{a+3} \ dx \\
&= (a+1)(a+2) \left[\frac{1}{a+3} x^{a+3} - \frac{1}{a+4}x^{a+4}\right]_0^1 = \frac{(a+1)(a+2)}{(a+3)(a+4)}
\end{align}
$$

## Ex: Nonlinear Expectation (3)

::: {.callout title="Example 11.15"}
Let the continuous random variable $X$ have the following PDF:

$$
f_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
6 x(1-x) &\text{for } x \in (0, 1) \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

Let $g(X) = \frac{1}{X}$. What is $\text{E}[g(X)] = \text{E}\left[\frac{1}{X}\right]$?

## Alternative View of Variance

::: {.callout title="Theorem 11.3"}
Let $X$ be a random variable. The variance of $X$, $\text{Var}[X]$, can be written as:

$$
\text{Var}[X] = \text{E}[X^2] - \text{E}[X]^2
$$
:::

## Alternative View of Variance (Proof)

The proof in the continuous case is as follows:

$$\begin{align}
\text{Var}[X] &= E\left[(X - \mu)^2\right] = \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}}(x - \mu)^2 \ f_X(x) \ dx \\
&=\int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} \left(x^2 - 2\mu + \mu^2\right) f_X(x) \ dx \\
&= \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} x^2 f_X(x) \ dx - 2\mu \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} x f_X(x) \, dx + \mu^2 \int_{x \in \mathcal{X}} f_X(x) \ dx \\
&= \text{E}[X^2] - 2\text{E}[X] \cdot \text{E}[X] + \text{E}[X]^2 \\
&= \text{E}[X^2] - \text{E}[X]^2
\end{align}$$

. . .

The proof in the discrete case is similar.

## Ex: Cont. Variance

::: {.callout title="Example 11.16"}
Let the continuous random variable $X$ have the following PDF:

$$
f_X(x) = 
\begin{cases}
3 x^2 &\text{for } x \in (0, 1) \\
0 &\text{otherwise}
\end{cases}
$$

What is $\text{Var}[X]$?
:::

. . .

We already know that $\text{E}[X] = \frac{3}{4}$. We find that $\text{E}[X^2]$ is

$$
\text{E}[X^2] = \int_0^1 x^2 \cdot 3 x^2 \ dx = \left[\frac{3}{5}x^5 \right]_0^1 = \frac{3}{5}
$$

Therefore, $\text{Var}[X]$ is

$$
\text{Var}[X] = \text{E}[X^2] - \text{E}[X]^2 = \frac{3}{5} - \frac{3^2}{4^2} = \frac{3}{80}
$$
